sentences.text: Females were larger than males, with estimated weights ranging from 10 to 18 kilograms for females and 9 to 12 kilograms for males.
A grown female had a wingspan estimated at up to 2.6 meters, though some estimates suggest it could reach 3 meters.
Its front-left talon measured between 4.9 and 6.15 centimeters, while the hallux-claw could reach up to 11 centimeters.
It was the largest eagle known to science and the largest known bird of prey, slightly larger than the largest vultures.
Māori legends described the bird as huge with black-and-white plumage, yellow-green tinged wings, and a red crest.
Its size and weight indicate that it exerted a striking force equivalent to a block of cement falling from the top of an eight-story building.
Julius von Haast first scientifically described the species in 1871 based on remains found by Frederick Richardson Fuller in an old swamp.
The species was named Harpagornis moorei in honor of George Henry Moore, who owned the Glenmark Estate where the bones were found.
Eight fossil occurrences have been recorded.
Its massive size evolved as a response to its primary prey, the flightless moa, which could weigh up to 200 kilograms.
The eagle predominantly preyed on large, flightless birds, frequently grabbing the prey's pelvis with one foot and killing it with a blow to the head or neck with the other foot.
A 2021 analysis indicated that the bill was functionally closer to that of the Andean condor than to other eagles.
Its main prey were moa, giant flightless birds unable to defend themselves against the impact force and speed of these eagles, which could reach speeds of 80 kilometers per hour.
Despite its short wingspan, evidence strongly suggests the bird was capable of flight.

The eagle's large size may have been an evolutionary response to its prey size, as it would have been substantially smaller when it arrived on the island before growing substantially over time due to a lack of competition.
Haast's eagles occupied the ecological niche of top mammalian predators in New Zealand.
Its large beak may also have been used to tear the internal organs of its prey, causing death by blood loss.
DNA analysis in 2005 showed the eagle was closely related to the smaller Australian and shrike-hawk species of the genus Hieraaetus, not the larger booted eagle as previously thought.
Consequently, Harpagornis moorei was renamed Hieraaetus moorei.
H. moorei may have diverged from these smaller hawks in a relatively recent period between 700,000 and 1.8 million years ago.

A later mitochondrial DNA study determined it was more closely related to the Australian goshawk than the shrike-hawk, with an evolutionary divergence from the Australian goshawk estimated at nearly 2.2 million years.
Its parent group is Accipitridae.
The species authority is listed as Haast, 1872.
Fossils of the species date from the Pleistocene to the Late Holocene.
The eagle went extinct around 1400 AD when its main food source, the moa, was hunted to extinction by Māori and its dense forest habitat was largely devastated.
Haast's eagles likely competed with Māori for food, and the eagle became extinct around the same time as its prey, the moa, which went extinct between 1440 and 1445.
It is debated whether Māori legends refer to Haast's eagle or to the extinct South Island Austral snipe.
Some researchers suggest the pouākai legend does not refer to Haast's eagle because the species is not known to have lived on the North Island.
Charles Edward Douglas claimed in his diaries that he encountered two enormous raptors in the Landsborough River valley, probably during the 1870s, and shot and ate them.
